{{nihongo|'''Takuzudama Shrine'''|多久頭魂神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Tsutsu, {{ill|Izuhara|Q11410123|qid=Q11410123}}, {{ill|Tsushima, Nagasaki|ar|تسوشيما (ناغاساكي)|az|Tsuşima (Naqasaki)|azb|تسوشیما، ناقاساکی|ca|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|ce|Цусима (Нагасаки)|de|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|es|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|fa|تسوشیما، ناگاساکی|fi|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|fr|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|it|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|ja|対馬市|ko|쓰시마시 (나가사키현)|mzn|تسوشیما، ناگازاکی|nl|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|no|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|pl|Tsushima (Nagasaki)|pt|Tsushima (cidade)|ro|Tsushima, Nagasaki|ru|Цусима (Нагасаки)|sv|Tsushima, Nagasaki|tg|Тсушима|tl|Tsusyima, Nagasaki|tr|Tsushima, Nagasaki|tt|Цусима (Нагасаки)|uk|Цушіма (Нагасакі)|ur|تسوشیما، ناگاساکی|vi|Tsushima, Nagasaki|war|Tsushima, Nagasaki|zh|對馬市|zh_classical|對馬市|zh_yue|對馬|qid=Q991032}}, {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture|Q169376|qid=Q169376}}. {{nihongo|'''Takuzudama Shrine'''|多久頭魂神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tsushima]].

== History ==
There is a tradition that the shrine was founded during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188}}, but this is considered a later attribution, and the precise date and circumstances of its establishment are unknown. In ancient times it was called “Takuzuda Shrine,” without the character for “tama” (soul). The “Takuzuda Shrine” listed among the thirteen shrines of Shimogata District, Tsushima Province, in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}} is identified with this shrine. Although the enshrined deities are said to be five deities including Amaterasu Ōmikami, the original deity was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Takuzuda-no-Kami}}, a god unique to {{ill|Tsushima Island|Q52051|qid=Q52051}}. In the entry for February 5, Jōwa 4 (837) in the 『{{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|Q1041301|qid=Q1041301}}』, there is a record of Takuzuto-no-Kami being promoted from no rank to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, which is thought to refer to the deity of this shrine. The shrine was part of Tsushima’s distinctive syncretic faith known as Tendō worship, which blended Shinto and Buddhism, and functioned together with a Kannon hall, where rituals were conducted by temple priests<ref>{{ill|Masataka Suzuki|Q11648975|qid=Q11648975}} “Rituals and Village Space in Tsutsu, Tsushima,” in *Cosmology of Ritual and Space—Tsushima and Okinawa*, Shunjūsha, 2004</ref>. Tendō worship is a syncretism of mother-and-child deity worship, sun worship, mountain worship, and other beliefs. Originally, the shrine had no sanctuary building and instead served as a place of distant worship of the sacred, restricted mountain Tendōyama (Tatera-yama). After the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535}} in the Meiji period, the Kannon hall of Tsutsutera, which had been a shrine temple, was used as the shrine building; however, this Kannon hall was destroyed by fire in 1956<ref>*Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Nagasaki Prefecture Place Names*, pp. 1011–1012, and *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten: Nagasaki Prefecture*, p. 595</ref>.

== Cultural properties ==
== Important Cultural Properties (national designation) ==
* **Bronze drum (Kinko)** — From the {{ill|Goryeo|Q28208|qid=Q28208}} period, made of bronze, diameter 81.2 cm. “Kinko” refers to what is known in Japan as a {{ill|Waniguchi|Q11674315|qid=Q11674315}}. It bears an inscription including “Zen-gen □ Mi fifth month day, Jinyang Prefecture,” as well as an additional inscription dated Shōhei 12 (1357). “Zen-gen” is thought to be a private era name, and “□ Mi” is considered to correspond to the yimi year (1245), the 32nd year of the reign of {{ill|Gojong of Goryeo|Q368892|qid=Q368892|lt=Gojong}}. It was produced in the same year in what is now {{ill|Jinju|Q42144|qid=Q42144|lt=Jinju City}}, {{ill|South Gyeongsang Province|Q41151|qid=Q41151}}, {{ill|South Korea|Q884|qid=Q884}}<ref name="#1">*Illustrated Guide to Newly Designated Important Cultural Properties 4: Crafts I*, pp. 166–167</ref>.
[[File:Bell of Takuzudama Shrine.jpg|thumb|230px|Temple bell]]
* **Temple bell** — A Japanese-style bell cast in Kōei 3 (1344) by metalworkers from Matsuura in Hizen Province. A long inscription appears in the pond-shaped section above the striking point, stating that the original bell was first made in Kankō 5 (1008) and was recast in Kōei 3 (1344). The craftsmen are identified as the master carpenter Kakuen and the assistant craftsman Suenaka from Yamashita Manor in Kamimatsuura, Hizen Province<ref name="#1"/>.
* **Goryeo-printed Tripitaka** — 3 volumes, 2 fascicles, 1,016 books (with appended *Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* [Japanese edition 318 fascicles, manuscript 6 fascicles], total 324 fascicles), designated in fiscal year 2017<ref>Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Notification No. 117, September 15, 2017</ref>.

== Theft incident ==
The “{{ill|List of TVB dramas in 2013|Q82800|qid=Q82800}}” that had been in the shrine’s possession was designated as a {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture cultural property|Q11652661|qid=Q11652661|lt=Nagasaki Prefecture cultural property}}<ref>[http://www.pref.nagasaki.jp/bunkadb/bunkazai_details_nomap.php?id=260 “Tripitaka of Takuzudama Shrine”]{{dead link|date=January 2018}} Nagasaki Prefecture, Cultural Properties of Nagasaki Prefecture</ref>, but it was stolen in October 2012 along with the “Standing Bronze Buddha Tathāgata” from {{ill|Kaijin Shrine|Q11559099|qid=Q11559099}} and the “Seated Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva” from {{ill|Kannon-ji Temple|Q11630602|qid=Q11630602|lt=Kannon-ji}} (the {{ill|Tsushima Buddha statue theft incident|Q18337378|qid=Q18337378}})<ref>[http://www.nagasaki-np.co.jp/kiji/20121010/02.shtml “Two additional cases of cultural property theft discovered”]{{dead link|date=January 2018}} {{ill|The Nagasaki Shimbun|Q11652567|qid=Q11652567}}, October 10, 2012</ref>. In January 2013, a group of {{ill|Korean nation|Q11271251|qid=Q11271251}} who attempted to bring the items into South Korea to sell them were detained, and the two Buddhist statues were recovered; however, the perpetrators stated that the Tripitaka had been “discarded in the fields and mountains around the shrine”<ref>[https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASDG3000V_Q3A130C1CR0000/ “Man detained in Tsushima Buddhist statue theft; South Korean police recover stolen items”] {{ill|The Nikkei|Q1077694|qid=Q1077694}}, January 30, 2013</ref>.
